events_chronological: Newsreel footage lays out the head of state's years in office, a failed invasion and a missile standoff.
On an autumn afternoon the head of state is shot dead in a plaza in a southern city.
A patrolman is shot dead nearby, and Dale Kerrigan is arrested in a cinema and charged with both killings.
Kerrigan denies everything, calls himself a patsy, and is shot by a club owner named Sy Poulos in the basement of police headquarters.
River-city district attorney Hollis Trent notices Kerrigan's local connections and interviews the pilot Duvall.
Federal agents take the case away from Trent, and he lets it go for three years.
The official commission publishes its single-bullet conclusion and twenty-six volumes of supporting evidence.
Three years later Trent reads the commission's report, finds it unbelievable, and reopens the investigation with his own staff.
Trent's team retrace Kerrigan's summer in the river city, his leafleting for a pro-regime committee and his links to the investigator Bannon's office above a coffee warehouse.
Witnesses describe shots from a grassy rise, men flashing badges behind a fence, and a rifle in a window.
Duvall, terrified and drinking, tells Trent he is a dead man, and is found dead a few days later.
A prisoner named Delmar describes a party at which a man called Vasse, Duvall and Kerrigan discussed killing the head of state.
Trent meets a man in the capital who gives his name only as a letter, and who describes how the security detail was stripped, who stood to gain, and how such an operation would be run.
Trent charges the businessman Emile Vasse with conspiracy, identifying him as the man Delmar named.
The press turns on Trent, his staff resign, his marriage nearly collapses, and his witnesses die or recant.
At trial Trent runs an amateur film of the shooting over and over and argues the physical impossibility of the single-bullet theory.
Trent delivers a closing address to the jury about a coup and about telling the truth.
The jury acquits Vasse in under an hour while accepting that there was a conspiracy.
Closing captions record that Vasse's intelligence connection emerged later, and that files remain sealed into the next century.
nonlinear_category_reason: The prosecutor's investigation and trial hold 12 of 15 scenes, and the assassination and the commission's findings are reconstructed from earlier.
syuzhet_notes: The present is the district attorney's investigation and trial, and nearly everything else arrives as reconstruction: told-order bullets 1-4 are newsreel and staged history, and bullets 9-12 are witness accounts staged as flashback, often in several mutually incompatible versions of the same afternoon. Told-order bullet 14, the meeting with the anonymous source, is a long flashback inside a flashback, and the film cuts speculative footage into documentary material throughout without marking where one ends and the other begins.
fabula_notes: Much of what is dramatised is conjecture presented as reconstruction - the film stages several versions of the shooting, only one of which can be true - so this chronology follows the account the prosecutor assembles rather than an established record. The meeting with the anonymous source and several of the witness scenes are composites invented for the film.
